questions.text: What does DOE require lighting designers to consider when coordinating daylight with artificial lighting?

options.text: Glare, brightness imbalance, and heat buildup in the building interior.
Only the color of furniture.
Only elevator waiting interval.
Only plumbing fixture count.

questions.rationale: Glare, brightness imbalance, and heat buildup in the building interior. This answer matches DOE Guidelines refined markdown lines 323-405.
questions.explanation: This describes a feature of internal shading (roller shades, blinds) that allows occupant control but provides minimal thermal benefit—the opposite of why external shading is superior. Color rendering index relates to light quality perception, not thermal performance; external shading's thermal advantage is independent of CRI specifications. Thermal mass and humidity reflection are not relevant mechanisms for external shading thermal performance; the cooling load reduction comes from preventing solar radiation ingress, not mass or humidity management. External louvers intercept solar radiation outside the building envelope, preventing heat gain before it enters the conditioned space. This is more effective than internal shading, which allows solar radiation to penetrate into the building and convert to internal heat. [Specific 40–60% reduction claim requires thermal simulation or code reference not provided in search results.] External shading strategy placement is critical in tropical design; intercepting radiation outside the envelope achieves superior thermal control, justifying higher initial cost through operational energy savings.

questions.text: Why is daylighting an envelope issue as well as a lighting issue?

options.text: Glazing has no effect on cooling load.
Larger glazing can admit more heat, so the envelope must control solar gains while allowing useful daylight.
Daylighting eliminates the need for window design.
The envelope affects plumbing only.

questions.rationale: Larger glazing can admit more heat, so the envelope must control solar gains while allowing useful daylight. This answer matches DOE Guidelines refined markdown lines 785-803.
questions.explanation: CFLs achieve 60–80 lm/W and have 10,000–20,000 hour lifespan; they do not match the 80–120 lm/W efficacy range or the high-bay suitability of HID systems. Linear fluorescent (T8/T5) achieves 60–80 lm/W with 10,000–20,000 hour lifespan; while similar to CFL in efficacy, they lack HID's superior efficiency and high-bay design capability. Incandescent lamps achieve only 12–15 lm/W efficacy, have extremely short 1,000-hour lifespan, and are prohibited in the Philippines for general illumination under energy code mandates. HID lamps (metal halide, high-pressure sodium) achieve 60–150 lm/W efficacy depending on type, with lifespans of 6,000–15,000 hours. Metal halide typically ranges 60–100 lm/W; high-pressure sodium ranges 80–150 lm/W., are ideal for high-bay industrial and outdoor applications, and exhibit color shift as they age—a characteristic distinguishing feature of HID technology. HID lamps remain relevant in high-bay industrial contexts where their superior efficacy justifies color-shift maintenance requirements; understanding technology trade-offs guides appropriate fixture selection across building types.

questions.text: According to DOE, when can daylighting energy savings outweigh added cooling penalty?

options.text: Whenever the window area is maximized without controls.
Only when all artificial lights are removed.
When the building envelope is carefully designed to allow daylighting while limiting excess solar gain.
Only when the room has no occupants.

questions.rationale: When the building envelope is carefully designed to allow daylighting while limiting excess solar gain. This answer matches DOE Guidelines refined markdown lines 785-803.
questions.explanation: Horizontal overhangs provide minimal shadow at 84–90° altitude; at summer solstice, tan(84–90°) produces minimal overhang projection, leaving the window exposed to direct radiation. While egg-crate louvers combine horizontal and vertical control, they are optimal for equinox periods (65–68° altitude). At summer solstice extremes, simple vertical fins are more effective and economical. Interior shading allows 60–80% solar radiation penetration; at summer solstice, direct radiation penetrates horizontally into the building, defeating occupant comfort and thermal control goals. At 84–90° solar altitude (near-vertical), the sun approaches directly overhead; vertical fins are most effective because they block the lateral radiation while allowing overhead-reflected diffuse light to penetrate. Horizontal overhangs become ineffective at high altitudes, projecting minimal shadow. Egg-crate configurations are optimal for equinox periods, not summer solstice extremes. Shading device effectiveness is latitude- and season-specific; summer solstice vertical designs differ fundamentally from equinox egg-crate or winter horizontal configurations—understanding solar altitude geometry is essential for tropical daylighting control.

questions.text: What should transparent envelope portions do in daylighting design?

options.text: Admit all direct solar gain without control.
Replace all artificial lighting controls.
Serve only as decorative facade elements.
Prevent solar gains above what is needed for effective daylighting.

questions.rationale: Prevent solar gains above what is needed for effective daylighting. This answer matches DOE Guidelines refined markdown lines 785-803.
questions.explanation: Decreasing setpoints would further reduce artificial lighting, allowing work-plane illuminance to fall below 400 lux during monsoon months, violating code requirements and occupant comfort. Fixed setpoints ignore monsoon variation; artificial lighting would not activate sufficiently to maintain design illuminance, resulting in visual discomfort and potential code non-compliance during high-cloud periods. Disabling daylight harvesting abandons energy savings opportunities and creates unnecessary artificial lighting dependency; the system should adapt, not surrender, to seasonal variation. During monsoon season, when baseline daylight factor decreases 20–30%, setpoints should be increased to 450–500 lux to trigger artificial lighting earlier and compensate for reduced natural light availability. This maintains the 400-lux work-plane target despite atmospheric changes, optimizing the balance between daylighting capture and artificial supplementation. Seasonal setpoint adjustment (±15–20%) is critical for tropical daylight harvesting performance; understanding how monsoon cloud cover requires higher triggering thresholds ensures consistent occupant comfort across seasonal transitions.

questions.text: What visible transmittance threshold applies when automatic daylighting control credit is taken?

options.text: Exactly 1.00 for every window.
Not more than 0.05.
Not less than 0.25 for the fenestration system where daylighting is applied.

questions.rationale: Not less than 0.25 for the fenestration system where daylighting is applied. This answer matches DOE Guidelines refined markdown lines 785-803.
questions.explanation: Solar altitude angles increase during summer solstice (June), but this would enhance daylighting penetration in north-facing spaces, not reduce it. The monsoon effect is atmospheric, not geometric. Building window orientation remains fixed; seasonal monsoon effects are meteorological (cloud cover) rather than architectural reorientation. While high humidity does cause surface condensation (reducing transmittance 30–50%), the 20–30% seasonal reduction in daylight factor is primarily due to cloud cover diffusing direct solar radiation. During the Southwest Monsoon (June–September), cloud cover increases and diffuse illumination dominates, causing daylight factor to decrease 20–30% relative to dry-season baseline. During monsoon season, cloud cover increases diffuse illumination uniformly across all orientations, but the reduction in direct solar radiation (which normally penetrates deeper into spaces) results in lower overall daylight factors. North-facing facades benefit from diffuse light but lose the penetration depth advantage of direct solar radiation. Tropical daylighting design must account for monsoon-induced atmospheric changes; lighting control systems require seasonal setpoint adjustments (±15–20%) to maintain consistent illuminance through differing cloud conditions.
